name: Going Up?
hook: The elevator is your party, your inventory, and your getaway vehicle.
loop: At each stop, inspect three floor buttons, choose a destination, open the doors, and resolve a short encounter. Recruit a passenger, salvage a module, or retreat before the doors close. Reach the rooftop with your strange little crew.
controls: Click a destination; drag passengers between six cabin spaces; play one passenger ability per turn. Encounters are turn-based, so this works on touch as well as desktop.
fun: People—not swords—make your build. A bellhop adds luggage storage. A botanist grows a vine into a secret floor. A sleepy giant grants strength but occupies two spaces. A ghost can pass through closed doors but refuses sunlit floors. Passenger friendships unlock combination abilities.
moment: The aquarium floor is flooding. Your botanist can seal the door, but the talking fish offers a shortcut if you carry its tank. Take the fish and lose a cabin slot, or keep space for the rooftop rescue?
rules: Weight is a visible resource, not a surprise punishment. Preview floor risks and offer a safe stop after difficult encounters. Losing a run unlocks new passenger stories; permanent unlocks add options rather than raw power.
mvp: One 2D cabin, eight authored floor encounters, six passengers, three modules, and a ten-stop run. Recombine authored encounters with seeded selection; do not build a whole explorable tower or generate dialogue with AI.
expand: Later: themed tower packs, daily seeds, passenger relationship collections, and asynchronous sharing of unusual cabin builds.
feasibility: Small–medium · strong first prototype · 10–15 minute runs

name: Escalator Orchestra
hook: Fit moving stairways together, then watch a shopping mall turn into a little people machine.
loop: A piece queue supplies escalators, landing bridges, and junctions. Rotate and place them on a side-view grid to connect entrances with destination floors. Press Play to send a passenger wave through your creation; pause, repair, and replay.
controls: Drag a piece, rotate with a button or keyboard, flip its travel direction, then run the simulation. Planning has no timer; an optional rush mode introduces a falling-piece countdown.
fun: Borrow the fitting-and-rotation appeal of falling-block puzzles, not the exact Tetris identity. Completing a useful route earns a new piece; floors do not disappear. Two passengers reaching different goals on the same beat create a musical combo. Carrying a balloon reveals overhead clearance problems.
moment: A red shopper needs floor 3, a blue shopper needs floor 2, and you have one long escalator left. A timed junction sends the first to the bridge and the second upward. The whole mall plays a satisfying two-note chord.
rules: Every escalator needs valid landings and clear space. Show direction arrows and predicted paths before Play. Add elevators or ramps for wheelchair routes; escalators are not treated as accessible substitutes.
mvp: A 10-by-8 grid, two passenger destinations, six piece types, deterministic passenger routing, and twelve handcrafted puzzles. A route graph drives the simulation; animated steps are only visual.
expand: Later: station interchanges, moving walkways, daily piece seeds, a sandbox, and shareable puzzles with a verified solution.
feasibility: Small · easiest elevator idea to ship · 2–5 minute puzzles

name: Shaft Sprint
hook: Race elevator cabins through a tower made of lanes, stops, and deliciously risky shortcuts.
loop: Accelerate up one of three shafts, brake precisely at transfer floors, slide through a connector, and choose your next shaft. Three short stages make a race. Optional delivery stops trade a few seconds for a useful upgrade.
controls: Hold to accelerate, release to brake, and tap left/right at a lit transfer gate. The cabin follows constrained rails; you are racing decisions and timing, not wrestling a free-flying vehicle.
fun: Draft behind another cabin for a charge boost. Nail a smooth stop for a slingshot departure. Pick a turbo battery, a one-use express pass, or a spring connector. A catch-up battery gives trailing racers tactical options without stealing steering control.
moment: The leader takes the straight express shaft. You brake at the laundromat, pick up a delivery battery, and use a diagonal maintenance connector to emerge one floor ahead.
rules: Transfers work only at marked gates, so routes stay readable. Start with AI and ghost races; leave online multiplayer and complex physics for later. Treat it as an original arcade game, not a Mario Kart reskin.
mvp: A side-on 2.5D tower, three shafts, one course, two AI opponents, three power-ups, and a time-trial ghost. Deterministic rail motion plus simple collision rules.
expand: Later: course editor, local split-screen, rotating tower themes, and sideways connectors. Upside-down racing is a late novelty, not the core control scheme.

name: Last Train Home
hook: Not every passenger is alive. Every passenger still deserves the right stop.
loop: Walk through a compact carriage, speak to passengers, inspect tickets and reflections, then choose a stop or transfer on the network map. Gather enough evidence to take each passenger home before the last connections close.
controls: Click objects and dialogue choices; pin clues to a notebook; select a route. A relaxed mode pauses the timetable while reading. Use text, symbols, and visible clues—not audio alone.
fun: Supernatural behavior follows discoverable rules. A ghost ticket names a station that was renamed. A passenger appears only in the window reflection. A musician repeats the same verse whenever you ride a loop. Your job is to understand them, not randomly accuse or eject them.
moment: A child holds an old ticket to a renamed station. The physical station still exists, but an evening newspaper and a changing map let you connect its old name to the new one. The child vanishes gently after the correct announcement.
rules: Every solution needs at least two supporting clues. Ordinary passengers can be unusual too; strange behavior is not proof of danger. Missing a connection opens another route or ending instead of silently making the case impossible.
mvp: One reusable carriage, six fictional stations, four authored mysteries, a clue notebook, and two endings. Reuse station backgrounds; do not recreate an entire city in 3D.
expand: Real-city packs reuse actual station order and transfers while placing explicitly fictional stories on top. Historical names require research; ghost platforms are visibly separated from real service information.

name: Rush Hour Rescue
hook: A train being on time is nice. A whole city making its connections is the real victory.
loop: Observe platform queues and train positions; add a spare train, adjust departures, briefly hold a connection, or turn a service back at an allowed terminal. Run the next few minutes and read the passenger consequences.
controls: Click a train or station on a schematic map, choose from valid dispatch actions, and use pause or speed controls. A visible forecast compares likely queue changes before committing.
fun: Solve competing needs rather than simply buying more trains. Event crowds leave one station, an airport connection approaches closing time, and another platform is filling. A helpful hold can save a transfer while causing a queue elsewhere.
moment: A concert ends near a stadium. You use a spare train to clear its platform, then hold a connecting line for 20 seconds. The departing wave becomes a glowing ribbon of passengers making their last transfer.
rules: Enforce simplified safe separation and platform capacity as hard constraints; never reward reckless train operation. Score passenger waiting and crowding alongside service reliability. This is a game model, not a professional dispatch trainer.
mvp: Two intersecting lines, twelve stations, one depot, aggregate passenger groups, and three scenarios. Use a discrete-event simulation and simplified dwell/headway rules, not individual commuter AI.
expand: Import licensed real-city topology and schedules where available. Add city-specific scenarios, demand presets, service-change planning, and an optional deeper operations model only when data supports it.
feasibility: Medium–large · most ambitious systems idea · 10–20 minute scenarios

name: One Ticket, Many Errands
hook: Turn a familiar subway map into a city-sized puzzle of tiny acts of kindness.
loop: Accept three errands, inspect station facilities and deadlines, plan a route, then ride and decide whether to get off or continue. Finish with limited time, a small bag, and the fewest unnecessary transfers.
controls: Click stations to queue a route, reorder errands, and choose actions at stops. Show predicted travel and transfer time, then reveal optional complications in a clearly labeled challenge mode.
fun: Deliver a cake without using the crowded peak service, return a lost umbrella, and catch a rooftop picnic before sunset. A fragile parcel prefers fewer transfers; a hot lunch wants the fastest arrival. Bonus clues lead you to a delightful station mural.
moment: Two errands point in opposite directions. Completing the umbrella delivery first unlocks a locker at the interchange, letting you stash the bulky parcel and take a faster loop to the picnic.
rules: Separate fictional errand deadlines from real timetables. Accessibility mode plans step-free paths only when the imported pack has validated accessibility information; otherwise label it unknown rather than assume.
mvp: A fictional 15-station network, eight errands, three item constraints, fixed travel times, and illustrated stop vignettes. A shortest-path solver provides hints rather than always choosing for the player.
expand: Best entry point for real-city packs: recognizable maps become playable with no detailed station models. Add local stories and landmarks from permitted sources; let players create purely fictional errands.
feasibility: Small · best first real-city-capable game · 5–10 minute trips

name: Transfer Garden
hook: Build an interchange that feels like a welcoming little garden, not a confusing maze.
loop: Place platforms, corridors, signs, escalators, elevators, and rest areas. Run a passenger wave, watch bottlenecks, then rearrange the station. Optimize different journeys rather than a single throughput number.
controls: Build on a compact grid; rotate pieces; select a passenger group to see its route. Toggle a crowd heatmap, step-free network, and walking-time overlay.
fun: Different travelers expose different design problems. A family needs a meeting spot, a visitor follows signs, and a wheelchair user needs a continuous lift route. Clever placement makes streams separate and rejoin like a choreographed dance.
moment: A short escalator clears one queue but floods a narrow bridge. Widening the bridge is expensive. Moving a sign and routing exiting passengers around a garden solves the jam while keeping the step-free route intact.
rules: Show pedestrian capacities and valid connections. Emergency routes are constraints, not score exploits. Optimize walking time, crowding, accessibility, and comfort; the prettiest station may not be the best one.
mvp: One fictional interchange, a 20-by-20 grid, six building tools, three traveler groups, and aggregate flow simulation. Do not simulate every person with expensive collision physics.
expand: Use real-city line/platform relationships to inspire stations, but label layouts as fictional unless independently sourced. Combine with Escalator Orchestra as its longer-form sandbox mode.
feasibility: Medium · naturally joins elevators and metro · 15–30 minute builds

name: The Missing Line
hook: An extra line appears on the map only after midnight. Discover its rules before it folds the city.
loop: Compare the normal network with a supernatural overlay; observe anomalous journeys; test a route hypothesis; mark which ghost connections are real. Rescue three stranded passengers using the rules you uncover.
controls: Click connections to mark a theory, take a test ride, and inspect a journey log. The entire game can live on a schematic map with short station vignettes.
fun: Treat the haunting as a solvable logic system. A ghost edge works only after changing line twice; a mirrored station reverses route direction; a ring closes only when visited clockwise. Rules are revealed through controlled experiments, not random jump scares.
moment: Your journey log says A → B took two minutes, but B → A took you to C. Comparing two rides reveals that the phantom shuttle advances one station each time the normal circle line crosses midnight.
rules: The generator chooses from a small tested rule library and verifies that objectives are reachable. Every anomaly is visually marked; the normal city graph remains unchanged and can always be inspected.
mvp: A ten-station fictional network, three authored anomaly rules, five puzzles, a hypothesis notebook, and one rescue objective per puzzle. Build a rule evaluator and reachability checker before procedural puzzles.
expand: Put the same rule system over real-city topology. Circles, branches, and interchange clusters create different puzzle shapes. Use a fictional overlay disclaimer and avoid pretending that imaginary stations are official.
feasibility: Small–medium · unusual and very map-friendly · 5–15 minute puzzles
